title: Synthesis and Characterization of Highly Stable Fisetin Encapsulated in Lecithin-Chitosan-Savie Nanoparticles

sections.abstract: Senolytic drugs, of the class of polyphenolic flavonoids, have attracted attention for a wide variety of medical applications for which they may be delivered topically, orally, and/or intravenously. However, due to their hydrophobicity and sensitivity to light and oxygen, they have been proven difficult to package and deliver. Here we report a synthesis method for encapsulated fisetin using lecithin-chitosan ionic gelation with a recently reported surfactant that is an alternative to polyethylene glycol (PEG)-containing compounds. Called “Savie” for a contraction of its components, sarcosine-Vitamin E, this surfactant allows for production of sub-100 nm nanoparticles that are bench stable for at least 10 months without aggregation. The environmentally sensitive fluorescence of fisetin allows it to be used as a tool for analysis of particle structure and stability. Absorbance, steady-state fluorescence, and fluorescence lifetime measurements alone and with quenchers indicate that a fraction of the fisetin is accessible to the surface solution and highly photooxidizable, whereas a second fraction is deeply complexed within the particle and significantly more stable. The two fractions may be distinguished from their absorbance peaks. The particles are readily taken up by cultured fibroblasts, with distinct fluorescence lifetimes occurring on the edges vs the interior of the cell. The particles show strong antioxidant activity in cells which is a combination of the effects of fisetin and Vitamin E.
sections.introduction:
Cellular senescence is one of the 12 hallmarks of aging. Senescent cells (SNCs) show replicative arrest with resistance to apoptosis and often increased metabolic activity. Some also display senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), where the cells secrete high levels of inflammatory cytokines, immune modulators, growth factors, and proteases. Senescent cells accumulate in many tissues with aging and at sites of pathology in multiple chronic diseases, including cancer, osteoarthritis and degenerative disk disease, Alzheimer’s disease, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. , Senescent cells also cause signs of intrinsic chronological aging, such as frailty, osteopenia, and skin changes. In healthy older adults, skin senescent cells increase dramatically between ages 60–80. − Along with skin dryness and wrinkling, the skin becomes more susceptible to cancer and shows delayed healing. , It has been proposed that “therapies that reduce the number of senescent cells or block SASP may be effective treatments for aging-associated skin deterioration”.

Therapeutic strategies aimed at safely interfering with the detrimental effects of cellular senescence, such as the selective elimination of SNCs or the disruption of the SNC secretome via senolytics, have been garnering significant research attention. , Senolytics are small active molecules that selectively induce apoptosis of senescent cells, and are an ideal therapeutic agent in that they induce death of aged cells in a normal, controlled manner, as would naturally occur in an organism.

Senolytic agents have been identified by bioinformatics approaches as well as high-throughput drug library screens. A large number of compounds, many from plants, have been identified as having senolytic activity; many of these fit within the general class of polyphenolic flavonoids. A subset of this class are the flavonols, which include quercetin, fisetin, rutin, and others ( Figure A). These compounds are highly redox active, accounting for their antioxidant activity, and are also hydrophobic, making them insoluble in water. Developing delivery mechanisms for stable, soluble formulations of flavonoids is thus a significant challenge. The most common delivery route is systemic and oral. There is an exploding market of ingestible senolytic supplements which have not been evaluated by regulatory agencies, as well as formulations in clinical trials. ,

Structures of (A) flavonol and (B) fisetin. (C) Different forms of fisetin occurring under varying solvent conditions with their emission peaks upon 370 nm excitation.

Fisetin ( Figure B), first extracted from venetian sumach ( Cotinus coggygria or smoke tree), has been shown to be an effective senolytic agent in wild-type mice, with effects of increased lifespan, reduced senescence markers in tissues, and reduced age-related pathologies. Fisetin induces apoptosis by inhibition of the antiapoptotic protein, and inhibits the activity of several pro-inflammatory cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor α, interleukin 6, and nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB). The anti-inflammatory action is due to deacylation of the pro-inflammatory transcription factor NF-κB by sirtuin 1. Fisetin has roughly twice the senolytic potency of quercetin. The photophysical properties of fisetin have been explored in several studies, demonstrating shifts in the excitation and emission spectra between the neutral, photoautomer, and anionic forms of the molecule ( Figure C).

One of the biggest unsolved questions in the field of senolytic research is that of deliverysystemic (usually oral), regional (e.g., injection into a joint), or topical. ,, Oral and topical therapies may complement each other, so the use of both may be recommended. A large number of cosmetics and cosmeceuticals have appeared in recent years that contain plant-based extracts containing polyphenols or purified polyphenols, , but these are mostly untested for activity or stability. Emulsions are the most common delivery vehicle for topical application.

Stabilization of polyphenols for delivery may be performed using micro-or nanoencapsulation. , Many methods for encapsulation of hydrophobic molecules are available: lipid micelles or liposomes, solid lipid nanoparticles, silica nanoparticles, nanogels, lecithin/chitosan particles, and others. These encapsulation techniques are widely used in medicine for delivery of hydrophobic anticancer drugs, and are of emerging interest for local and systemic treatment of skin cancers and other skin conditions. , Skin presents specific barriers to delivery; any nano- or microparticle formulation for skin must be able to penetrate the stratum corneum, placing specific demands on particles not seen with injectable formulations.

Most reported stable polyphenol preparations contain ethoxylated surfactants such as polyethylene glycol (PEG) and its derivatives. For example, the vitamin-E based D-α-tocopheryl polyethylene glycol (TPGS) has been reported in fisetin encapsulation to enhance anticancer properties of fisetin in breast cancer cell assays. Quercetin has also been encapsulated in nanoparticles containing TPGS. , A second-generation surfactant, TPGS-750-M, is especially prevalent in medicinal chemistry reactions. ,

However, PEGs are not readily biodegradable and hence pose environmental concern, and may also cause side effects such as immunogenicity; , they also form peroxides upon prolonged exposure to air, which can damage encapsulation structures such as liposomes. Because of these concerns, there are emerging efforts to provide alternatives. A recent report of a new PEG-free surfactant called Savie provides an alternative to PEGs and in particular to TPGS. Named for “sarcosine + Vitamin E,” Savie has the same lipophilic moiety as TPGS (tocopherol) but uses a polysarcosine polypeptide as the alternative to PEG.

Savie has been reported in several subsequent studies on micellar catalysis, , but to our knowledge, this is the first study using Savie-based nanoparticles in cell targeting applications. This study reports synthesis and photophysical characterization of lecithin-chitosan-Savie nanoparticles containing fisetin and delivery of the encapsulated fisetin to cultured fibroblasts, with analysis of the stability of the encapsulated fisetin over a period of ten months.
sections.results:
Fisetin encapsulated in lecithin-chitosan alone, without surfactant, resulted in elongated, micron-sized particles that precipitated from solution within several days ( Supporting Information Figure S1 ). When Savie was added to the synthesis, the nanoparticle emulsion was translucent in appearance and did not precipitate. No discrete particles could be visualized under fluorescence microscopy.

Encapsulation efficiency is often performed using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). However, because of its bright fluorescence, the encapsulation of fisetin could be estimated using a fluorescence-based assay. After separation of nanoparticles from unencapsulated fisetin by centrifugation, the weight of fisetin in the unencapsulated supernatant was estimated as WT­(SUP). Encapsulation efficiency EE was then calculated as

Using this approach, the encapsulation efficiency was estimated at 96 ± 3% for 3 independent measurements, which corresponded to ∼0.38 mg/mL of fisetin expected in the undiluted capsules before dialysis.

Negatively stained TEM images showed a fairly homogeneous distribution of round nanoparticles ( Figure A,B). Dynamic light scattering (DLS) analysis gave particle sizes of (mean ± standard deviation) 100 ± 35 for freshly prepared particles before dialysis, 97 ± 49 for freshly prepared particles after dialysis, and 94 ± 10 for particles aged on the benchtop for 10 months ( Figure C–E). The ζ potential was positive in 15 mM NaCl, 25.0 ± 0.1 mV for an average of 3 measurements.

Size and dispersion of particles. (A, B) TEM images of negatively stained particles. (C) Particle size distribution before and after dialysis.

Absorbance spectra of fresh particles showed a distinct peak at 370 nm identical to the peak of fisetin in ethanolic solution. The amount of fisetin lost during dialysis estimated using this peak was approximately 22% ( Figure A), leaving a concentration of 0.25 mg/mL in fresh dialyzed particles as estimated by the A 370 peak. The fisetin-containing particles also showed a smaller absorbance feature at 320 nm. Neither of these features was seen in empty lecithin-chitosan-Savie nanoparticles, which absorbed primarily in the ultraviolet. As the particles aged at room temperature, the peak at 370 nm disappeared more quickly than the peak at 320 nm ( Figure B). Strong complexing of the flavonol with nanoparticles has been reported to lead to disappearance of the primary absorbance feature at 370 nm with both fisetin and quercetin. Thus, a small but significant fraction of tightly complexed fisetin remained in aged particles, which could be estimated using the secondary absorbance peak. The molar extinction coefficients of the two peaks were calculated here in ethanol as 16.2 ± 0.5/mM cm at 370 nm and 7.7 ± 0.2/mM cm at 320 nm. Using these values yielded a significant discrepancy between concentrations calculated with each peak as the particles aged. Values measured using UPLC-MS corresponded to the A 320 peak in the particles aged 10 months, but overestimated the concentration in particles aged 3 months ( Table ).

Absorbance and emission. (A) A reduction in the primary absorbance feature at 370 nm is seen with dialysis and may be used to estimate concentration. (B) Absorbance of fresh dialyzed nanoparticles and 10 month aged nanoparticles with fisetin, plotted against empty lecithin-chitosan-Savie nanoparticles without fisetin and pure fisetin in ethanol solution. The arrow indicates the only peak seen in the aged particles and the secondary peak seen in the fresh particles. Inset: photo of freshly synthesized particles with fisetin (+fis) and empty. (C) Emission of nanoparticles vs fisetin in solution (arbitrary y -axis). Inset: fluorescence transillumination image (excitation 312 nm) of fresh nanoparticles and nanoparticles aged 10 months. The backgrounds are the same; increased exposure time in the aged particles shows background light from the transilluminator.

ND = not done.

The solution of freshly synthesized particles was highly fluorescent under UV transillumination; particles aged for ten months did not change their visible appearance and preserved significant amounts of fluorescence. Both fresh and aged particles showed fluorescence emission corresponding to the fisetin photoautomer form with a peak at 545 nm; a secondary peak at 470 nm was seen in ethanol but not in the nanoparticles ( Figure C). Because the emission is sensitive to environment, reliable quantification of concentrations could not be performed using the emission intensity. However, quantum yields of 545 nm emission at 374 nm excitation were 44% for the fresh particles and 31% for particles aged 10 months when measured against Coumarin 153 as a standard.

Increasing the sample temperature from 23 °C ambient to 45 °C led to a 50 ± 2% reduction in the emission of fresh nanoparticles ( N = 3 replicates), but only a 14 ± 3% reduction for 10-month-old particles ( N = 3) ( Figure A). Fresh particles showed significant, nonlinear quenching at 20–50 mM concentrations of potassium iodide (KI), while the aged particles showed <10% reduction in I 0 / I even at 50 mM, and a response that was linear over the 1–50 mM range ( Figure B). KI did not cause significant changes in fluorescence lifetime, indicating static quenching, though it did make the two-component lifetime fits somewhat less precise ( Supporting Information Figure S2 ).

(C) Ln­( I 0 / I ) vs time for UV exposure at 900 μW/cm 2 . The lines are fits to eq (2) as discussed in the text.

All fluorescence decays from encapsulated fisetin could be fit to a dual exponential. The narrow emission filter used ensured that these two components both represented the 545 nm photoautomer emission under different environmental conditions. Both ⟨τ i ⟩ and ⟨τ a ⟩ were greater in the aged particles than the fresh particles ( Figure A). The longer lifetime, τ 2 , of ∼6 ns showed virtually no change as the particles aged. The shorter lifetime, τ 1 , of 2–3 ns, was faster in the aged particles ( Figure B). This meant that the overall longer lifetime had to be due to a significantly higher ratio of longer to shorter lifetime in the aged particles. Indeed, the fresh particles had an amplitude fraction of only ∼0.5 for the longer lifetime, while this fraction was ∼0.8 for the aged particles. The effects of temperature on amplitude fraction were opposite in the fresh vs aged particles: increasing temperature increased the amplitude fraction of the longer lifetime in the fresh particles, but slightly reduced it in the aged particles ( Figure C). Mean values for 3–4 replicates are given in Table ; all values are provided in Supporting Information Table S1 . The average lifetimes found here were very similar to those reported previously in dimyristoylphosphatidylcholine (DMPC) vesicles, except that the decrease in lifetime with temperature in the DMPC was much more marked, falling from 5.0 ns at 15 °C to 2.9 ns at 35 °C. This was not surprising, as DMPC undergoes a phase change from solid gel to liquid crystal within this temperature range, and simply emphasizes that the lecithin-chitosan-Savie nanoparticles do not change markedly in fluidity across the temperature ranges studied here.

Values shown are means ± standard errors for N = 3 or 4 measurements. For all values, see Table S1.

DPPH is a stable free radical with an absorbance peak at 517 nm, appearing purple. In presence of antioxidants its odd electron becomes paired, resulting in loss of this peak and a shift of its visible appearance from purple to yellow. The antioxidant Trolox may be used as a standard to decolorize DPPH, and the efficacy of any given antioxidant expressed as the Trolox equivalent antioxidant capacity (TEAC) as given by

where the IC 50 of each compound is the concentration required for half-maximal decolorization activity.

On 3 separate experiments run on 3 separate days, we found that the 50% activity concentration of Trolox was 45.3 ± 0.6 μg/mL ( Supporting Information Figure S3A ). For pure fisetin, the results were more variable, with values of 17 ± 2 μg/mL found in 3 experiments ( Figure S3B ). The TEAC for pure fisetin was thus 2.7 ± 0.3, in excellent agreement with literature results of 2.80 ± 0.06. For the nanoparticles, 3 replicates were performed on the same day. The fresh nanoparticles showed 50% activity at a dilution factor of 0.091 ±. 004, or approximately an 11-fold dilution, meaning that the undiluted particles had the antioxidant capacity of (17 ± 2 μg/mL)/dilution factor, or 190 ± 20 μg/mL of pure fisetin, in very good agreement with the 250 μg/mL measured with absorbance (both peaks) and 190 μL/mL measured using UPLC-MS. The 10-month aged particles had 50% activity at a dilution factor of 0.48 ±. 07, or equivalent to 35 ± 4 μg/mL of fisetin, compared with the 15 μg/mL calculated from absorbance at 320 nm and UPLC-MS ( Figure S3C ). DPPH was chosen for this assay because it is commonly reported in the literature, allowing for a comparison with values using free fisetin and other types of encapsulated fisetin. ,− However, DPPH is not the only antioxidant assay available in vitro , and not a good measure of what antioxidant activity might be expected in vivo ; the DPPH assay also presents several kinetic and chemical pitfalls. We thus used it only as a method of comparing fisetin concentration with absorbance and UPLC-MS measurements. A cell-based assay was used to evaluate effects in living cells (see below).

When monitored using widefield fluorescence, cultured fibroblasts could be seen to exhibit noticeable fisetin fluorescence even over the background within 5–10 min of nanoparticle addition. There was strong perinuclear labeling suggesting endosomal uptake ( Figure A,B). Co-labeling the particles with rhodamine lipid showed that the majority of fisetin was still associated with the particles after cell uptake, although some free fisetin was seen, particularly near the cell membrane ( Figure C). In fluorescence lifetime images, fisetin around the exterior cell membrane was associated with a very distinct short lifetime of <1 ns, while fisetin inside the cells had a lifetime of ∼2 ns, varying slightly in different cell compartments ( Figure D, Table ). A phasor plot showed a clear separation of these two forms of fisetin ( Figure E). There were no apparent qualitative differences between fresh and aged particles in the cell experiments (not shown). Cytotoxicity was not observed at these short incubation times, but a full investigation remains to be performed on different cell lines, including cancer cells vs healthy primary cells and cells driven to senescence by serial passaging, radiation, or exposure to chemotherapeutic agents. −

Fluorescence images of Savie nanoparticle-fisetin uptake in mouse embryonic fibroblasts. Scale bar = 10 μm. (A) Cells after 10 min incubation, using a DAPI excitation/GFP emission filter cube. (B) Overlay of fisetin fluorescence and brightfield. (C) Fisetin encapsulated in 1% rhodamine lipid showing the fisetin channel in green, the rhodamine lipid channel in red, and the overlay which shows some free fisetin near the cell membrane. (D) Fluorescence lifetime image showing distinct short lifetime around the edges of the cell. (E) Phasor plot of panel (D) showing two distinct features.

The fluorescent cellular oxidant indicator CellRox Orange was used to measure antioxidant performance of the nanoparticles in cells compared with fisetin alone and a positive control, N -acetylcysteine (NAC), as recommended by the manufacturer’s protocol. Oxidative stress was induced by incubation with tert-butyl hydroperoxide, and negative controls included cells incubated with buffer only or empty nanoparticles. Cells incubated with NAC, fisetin alone, and nanoparticles all showed a reduction of the CellRox Orange fluorescence; this corresponded to a reduction in the number of fluorescent cells as well as to a decrease in signal per cell ( Figure A). Fluorescence curves showed a reduction in peak (and equivalent area under the curve) in a concentration-dependent manner. However, the antioxidant activity of the nanoparticles was significantly greater than that of fisetin alone, and empty nanoparticles showed substantial antioxidant activity, probably because cell esterases are able to cleave the Savie to release free tocopherol, as is seen with TPGS ( Figure B).

(B) Representative curves of CellRox Orange fluorescence with the addition of no antioxidant or with a positive control antioxidant (0.5 or 5 mM NAC or 20 μg/mL fisetin in DMSO) or with different concentrations of nanoparticles (NPs). Triplicates of four independent runs on three independent cell preparations yielded consistent curves for all antioxidants. Responses were normalized to a negative control containing no antioxidant, and a maximal response curve occurring at the highest dose of NAC or nanoparticles, where no peak was apparent. The fraction reduction in this normalized fluorescence peak was fit to a dose–response curve

where [ C ] is antioxidant concentration, and IC 50 is the antioxidant concentration at half-maximal inhibition. Using this formula for 3 different biological replicates (different cell cultures on different days) yielded an IC 50 of NAC of 0.7 ± 0.2 mM, and of fisetin alone of 15 ± 5 μg/mL (0.05 ± 0.02 mM) ( Supporting Information Figure S4 ). For the nanoparticles, IC 50 values measured as volume of particles added per mL of cell suspension were 4.8 ± 0.9 μL/mL for fresh particles, and 5.5 ± 0.9 μL/mL for particles aged 3 months. These values included the effects of both fisetin and the empty nanoparticles. At the lowest concentrations tested, the empty nanoparticles were as effective as the fisetin-containing particles. However, the empty particle effect plateaued with concentration ( Figure C). When normalized to an equal volume of empty nanoparticles, the IC 50 of fisetin could be estimated as 6 ± 1 μg/mL in fresh nanoparticles containing 191 μg/mL fisetin, still lower than that seen with fisetin alone, which may reflect increased bioavailability as has been seen in other studies or synergistic effects with the tocopherol. The particles aged 3 months fit to a straight line; when the value of fisetin concentration measured by UPLC-MS was used (71 μg/mL), half-maximal response occurred at 5 ± 1 μg/mL ( Figure D).
sections.conclusion:
This study examined the use of a newly reported surfactant, Savie, for encapsulation of fisetin for delivery to cells. We found that the capsules were remarkably stable, showing no significant change in size after ten months of storage in water under ambient conditions and retaining significant fluorescence and antioxidant activity.

All of the data are consistent with one fraction of the fisetin being tightly complexed in the particles, and another fraction more accessible to the solution ( Scheme ).

The accessible fraction is quenched by potassium iodide and disappears as the particles age. The tightly complexed fraction is stable over many months and shows significant fluorescence and some antioxidant activity. It does not show the absorbance peak at 370 nm but retains a peak at 320 nm. The tightly complexed fraction likely corresponds to an increased fluorescence lifetime of close to 6 ns, which represents 80% of the amplitude of the decay in the aged particles. The antioxidant capacity as measured by DPPH is consistent with the concentration estimated by A 320 and UPLC-MS. It must be noted that the quantum yield calculation for the aged particles appeared artificially high because there was no apparent absorbance peak at 374 nm.

The Savie particles are taken up rapidly by cultured fibroblasts. The fisetin is released from the lipid as indicated by distinct partitioning of fisetin fluorescence and labeled phosphatidylcholine. Fluorescence lifetimes in the cell membrane were markedly shorter than inside the cells. The nanoparticles show strong antioxidant activity in cells, with empty nanoparticles showing an approximately half-maximal effect that plateaus with concentration. The fisetin-containing nanoparticles show additional concentration-dependent antioxidant activity with an IC 50 lower than that seen of fisetin alone, indicating high bioavailability, consistent with previous results using a variety of other nanoencapsulation techniques.

Future work will involve quantifying senolytic activity of the particles in vitro and in vivo using different cell lines and animal models. Other hydrophobic molecules, such as chemotherapeutic agents often encapsulated using TPGS, , may also be encapsulated using Savie and will be the subject of future investigations.
